title: Array Name vs Pointer
concept: Array names are used like pointers, but are not true pointer variables.

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
Header for outputting `printf` and `sizeof` results.

The goal this time is to verify that array names and pointer variables are different even if they look similar.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
Program starting point. An array `arr` (20 bytes) and a pointer `p` (the size of the pointer) are prepared on the stack.

The important thing is that although both appear to be "address-related", they are different: `arr` is the data block itself, and `p` is a variable holding the address.

steps.title: array declaration
steps.explanation:
`int arr[5];` creates 5 consecutive int spaces.

The array name `arr` represents the data block itself and does not imply independent storage like a pointer variable.

steps.title: Assigning an array name to a pointer
steps.explanation:
In `int *p = arr;`, `arr` is converted to `&arr[0]` and stored in `p`.

The usage seems similar, but the type properties differ in `sizeof` and whether assignment is possible.

steps.title: Difference 1: sizeof result
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(arr)` returns the total number of bytes in the array, and `sizeof(p)` returns the size of the pointer variable.

This difference is the clearest evidence that arrays and pointers are different types.

steps.title: Size of pointer variable
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(p)` returns **the size of the pointer variable itself**. This value may vary depending on the environment (32/64 bit) and is independent of the target size pointed to by `p`.

So it is normal for `sizeof(arr)` and `sizeof(p)` to be different, and this difference is key evidence that arrays and pointers are different types.

steps.title: Difference 2: Reallocation possible?
steps.explanation:
The pointer `p` is a variable, so it can be reassigned to a different address.

On the other hand, array names cannot be replaced in the same way because they are not subject to assignment.

steps.title: Array name is a constant
steps.explanation:
`arr = p;` is a compilation error. Array names are not modifiable pointer variables.

The correct expression is "array names decay to pointers depending on the context".

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
Exit with `return 0;`.

Summary: The result of `sizeof` and whether it can be reassigned distinguishes arrays/pointers.

quiz.question: What do the array name `arr` and the pointer `p` have in common?
options: Both can be used as expressions representing address values.
quiz.explanation: Both can be dereferenced like `*arr`, `*p`, or indexed like `arr[i]`, `p[i]` (due to the Decay property).

misconceptions.correct: An array is an array, and a pointer is a pointer.
misconceptions.why:
When an array name is used in an expression, it simply ‘decays’ into a pointer.
If you take a picture of `sizeof`, its true color will be revealed.

keyTakeaway: Array names are constant addresses, and pointers are variable addresses. `sizeof` results are different!
